title: Social Media Use and Depressive Symptoms During Early Adolescence
authors: Nagata JM, Otmar CD, Shim J, Balasubramanian P, Cheng CM, Li EJ, Al-Shoaibi AAA, Shao IY, Ganson KT, Testa A, Kiss O, He J, Baker FC

primary_models.name: Unconstrained random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) of social media time and CBCL depressive raw score across 4 annual waves, with fixed sociodemographic and family covariates
primary_models.location_in_paper: Results, Within-Person Associations and Between-Person Association (pp. 5-6); Figure 2 (p. 6); full parameter table is eTable 3 in Supplement 1 (not bundled in this PDF); model fit comparison in Results p. 4-5 and eTable 1; interpreted in Abstract, Key Points, Discussion pp. 6-7 and Conclusions p. 7.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal panel with 4 annual waves (baseline, year 1, year 2, year 3; ABCD 5.1, follow-up through 2022). Social media time and depressive symptoms are both measured at every wave and modeled reciprocally. Latent random intercepts separate stable between-person differences from within-person (state-like) deviations; autoregressive and cross-lagged paths are estimated among the within-person components, plus within-wave residual covariances. The final model is the unconstrained RI-CLPM, which lets cross-lagged paths differ across intervals, so each interval (baseline to year 1, year 1 to year 2, year 2 to year 3) gets its own estimate in both directions. The authors compared this against a traditional CLPM (poor fit) and a constrained RI-CLPM before retaining the unconstrained version as final.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study release 5.1, 21 US sites, baseline recruited October 2016 to October 2018. Analytic sample N = 11,876 after excluding participants missing baseline age or sex assigned at birth; all available data retained at each wave via full information maximum likelihood, so wave-specific Ns vary (social media use: 11,832 baseline, 11,175 year 1, 10,370 year 2, 10,301 year 3; depressive symptoms: 11,859, 11,199, 10,895, 10,093; Table 2). Mean (SD) age at baseline 9.9 (0.6) years; 5680 (47.8%) female, 6196 (52.2%) male. Race and ethnicity (parent report): 709 (6.0%) Asian, 2392 (20.1%) Black, 2027 (17.0%) Hispanic or Latino, 410 (3.4%) Native American, 6166 (51.9%) White, 171 (1.4%) other. Household income from <=$24,999 (13.8%) to >=$200,000 (10.5%); parent highest education college or more 2039 (17.2%), high school or less 9799 (82.8%) as printed in Table 1.
primary_models.iv: In the SM-to-depression direction, the IV is youth-reported time spent on social media, ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, administered each year. Hours and minutes per weekday and weekend day were combined as [(weekday mean x 5) + (weekend mean x 2)]/7 = mean daily hours. Descriptives (Table 2, untransformed hours/day, M (SD)): baseline 0.12 (0.42), year 1 0.22 (0.60), year 2 0.68 (1.54), year 3 1.21 (2.05). Table 2 footnote states the social media variables were transformed in the final analytic model because years 0-1 were reported in ordinal categories and years 2-3 in continuous hours (0-24); the exact transformation is described only in Supplement 1. In the reverse direction, social media time at the next wave is the DV. The focal predictor in each cross-lagged path is the within-person deviation from the person's own mean, not raw hours.
primary_models.dv: Caregiver-reported CBCL DSM-oriented depressive problems scale, raw score (sum of items, not t-score), each year. Descriptives (Table 2, M (SD)): baseline 1.27 (2.01), year 1 1.39 (2.19), year 2 1.50 (2.30), year 3 1.69 (2.52). In the reverse direction the depressive score is the predictor of the next wave's social media time. Within-person deviations are modeled.

primary_models.equation: Observed: SM[i,t] = mu_SM[t] + RI_SM[i] + w_SM[i,t] (+ fixed covariates); DEP[i,t] = mu_DEP[t] + RI_DEP[i] + w_DEP[i,t] (+ fixed covariates), t = 0,1,2,3. Within-person: w_SM[i,t] = a_t*w_SM[i,t-1] + c_t*w_DEP[i,t-1] + u_SM[i,t]; w_DEP[i,t] = b_t*w_DEP[i,t-1] + d_t*w_SM[i,t-1] + u_DEP[i,t], t = 1,2,3; cov(u_SM[i,t], u_DEP[i,t]) estimated each wave; cov(RI_SM, RI_DEP) estimated. Focal: d_t (SM -> later depression) and c_t (depression -> later SM), freely estimated per interval. Covariates: sex, race/ethnicity, income, parental education, ACEs, parental monitoring, family conflict, study site.
primary_models.estimation: Structural equation model in lavaan, R version 4.4.2; maximum likelihood with robust SEs (MLR) and scaled test statistic; full information maximum likelihood for missing outcome data. No survey weights reported. Final unconstrained RI-CLPM fit: CFI 0.977, TLI 0.968, RMSEA 0.031 (90% CI 0.029-0.033), SRMR 0.022. Traditional CLPM: CFI 0.917, TLI 0.807, RMSEA 0.132; constrained RI-CLPM: CFI 0.966, TLI 0.957, RMSEA 0.036, SRMR 0.027. Two-sided P < .05; no multiple-comparison correction reported. Standardized cross-lagged effects interpreted against Orth et al benchmarks (small 0.03, medium 0.07, large 0.12). No sex or other interaction/stratified analyses reported in the main text.

d_transformation.native_metric: beta_std (standardized SEM path coefficients and standardized covariances)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (guidelines §4a, SEM standardized path). Applied to CI endpoints for d CI.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 SD within-person deviation in social media time (from the person's own mean) at wave t, in SD units of within-person deviation in depressive symptoms at wave t+1 (and the reverse for depression -> SM paths); covariances are correlations
d_transformation.notes: Estimates are already standardized, so SD_IV / SD_DV are not needed; sd_iv/sd_dv left null. Table 2 (p. 5) gives untransformed SDs for reference, but the social media variables were transformed in the final model (method described only in Supplement 1), so those SDs do not correspond to the modeled metric. Standardization is of within-person latent deviations, so the derived d reflects within-person effects and is not directly comparable to between-person per-SD-of-hours d's from other papers. Year-2 residual covariance (0.08) is read off Figure 2 without CI. Random-intercept covariance sign differs between text (-0.01) and Figure 2 (r = 0.01). [complete-stage check 2026-10-01] Full PDF re-read (10 pages, no supplement bundled). All printed CIs/exact ps already captured; p for '<.001' cells set to null with p_label. No SEs, z, or exact p for <.001 cells printed anywhere in the article; eTables 1-3 are in Supplement 1 only.

extraction_flags:
1. The PDF has only the 10-page article. Supplement 1 (eMethods, eTables 1-3) is not included, so the full parameter table (eTable 3), the covariate effects (eTable 2) and the transformation applied to the social media variable all come from the main text and Figure 2 only.
2. The paper does not say how social media time was transformed in the final model (years 0-1 were reported in ordinal categories, years 2-3 in continuous hours). The Table 2 SDs are untransformed, so sd_iv/sd_dv are left null. That is fine because the betas are already standardized.
3. The random-intercept covariance sign does not match: the text and Abstract print -0.01 (95% CI -0.04 to 0.02, P = .46), but Figure 2 labels it r = 0.01. I used the text value.
4. The year-2 within-wave residual covariance (r = 0.08) comes only from the Figure 2 label. It is drawn in black (significant), but no CI or p is printed.
5. Coders should decide whether the non-directional covariances (the random-intercept covariance and the year-2 and year-3 residual covariances) belong in the matrix or should be struck. The 6 cross-lagged paths are the core estimates.
6. The derived d from standardized within-person RI-CLPM paths is a within-person effect. It is not comparable to between-person d per SD of hours from other papers.
7. Table 1 prints parent education as college or more 17.2% and high school or less 82.8%. That looks inverted, but I copied it as printed.
8. p values printed as <.001 are stored as 0.001, with p_label "<.001".
